### I.

The wonders of the Lord seem cast without order or design into the field of immensity.

They shine scattered like those countless flowers with which spring enamels our meadows.

Let us not seek a more regular plan to describe them. Principle of all beings, everything belongs to you. <note>The author addresses God as the fundamental source or "Principle" from which all life flows.</note>

It is their secret connection with you that constitutes their value, regardless of the place or rank they occupy.

I shall dare to raise my gaze even to the throne of your glory. My thoughts will be vivified <note>Meaning to be "brought to life" or "animated."</note> by considering your love for mankind, and the wisdom that reigns within your works.

Your word <term>Word: In this mystical context, "The Word" (Parole) refers to the Logos or the creative power of God used to bring the universe into existence.</term> was subdivided at the origin, like a torrent which, from the height of the mountains, plunges down upon sharp rocks.

Be blessed, brilliant light, visible splendor of the eternal light, from which my thought received its existence.

If my thought were not one of your sparks, I would not have the power to contemplate you. <note>original: "étincelles" — Saint-Martin uses the "spark" metaphor common in mysticism to describe the divine origin of the human soul.</note>

Famous men, say no more: "the light of a torch communicates itself to other torches without decreasing," and it is thus that spirits are produced by God. <note>Saint-Martin is likely addressing Enlightenment philosophers who used physical analogies to explain spiritual phenomena without acknowledging the divine essence.</note>

Dishonor the visible light no more by speaking to us only of its material mechanism.

The torch depicts the life of maintenance, and not the law of generation. <note>original: "vie d'entretien" — meaning the way life is sustained or kept up, rather than how it is originally brought into being.</note>

Does it not require a substance outside of this torch for it to communicate visible light to it?

Why do the wise and the prudent cherish light? It is because they know that light and the soul of man are two torches that can never be extinguished.

And you, <term>Supreme Agent<note>original: "agent suprême" — In the author's mystical system, this refers to the active divine principle or God acting upon the universe.</note></term>, why can you not cease to penetrate all things, to see all things, and to carry your clarity everywhere?

It is because the holy oil drawn from your source is scattered throughout all regions, and your light finds everywhere a nourishment that belongs to it.

### 3.

I have cast my gaze upon nature. Rivers, where do you run with such impetuosity?

We go to help fill the <term>abyss<note>original: "l'abyme" — Often representing the chaotic or fallen state of reality that must be redeemed or "filled."</note></term>, and to bury iniquity beneath the waters.

We go to extinguish these volcanoes, these smoking embers which are like the remains of the great fire. <note>The "great fire" likely refers to a primordial spiritual catastrophe or the "Fall" of man, a central theme in Saint-Martin's philosophy.</note>

When we have accomplished this work, our springs will stop.

The silt will gather in the depths.

Fertile plains will rise in the place of precipices.

Herds will graze in peace in the places where voracious fish once swam;

Life strives everywhere to manifest itself; all disorder was originally foreign to nature.

The soul of man displays fertility everywhere; it shows everywhere that it is made for life.

It also carries within it traces of the horrible convulsions <note>In this mystical context, "convulsions" likely refers to the spiritual trauma or the "Fall" that separated the human soul from its original divine state.</note> it has suffered.

->4.<-

**MAN**, would you wish to afflict your friend? Would you not want to renounce causing your friend <note>The "friend" here may refer to a spiritual companion or, more likely in this tradition, the Divine Presence within, which the author suggests is pained by human ignorance.</note> to suffer?

Yet He suffers, so long as man does not seek to know the nature of the Lord’s work.

Who then could conceive of the suffering that <term>transgressors<note>The original French "prévaricateurs" refers to those who neglect their spiritual duties or wander from the path of divine truth.</note></term> must cause God, when they carry their wanderings so far as to act against Him?

No, man, you could not bear the sight of such an overwhelming picture. Who but God would have the strength for it?

Thus, it is He alone who forgives, and it is from Him alone that we learn charity.

# MAN

Walk the paths of this school every day, if you wish to learn what the Lord's work truly is.

May the master who teaches there find in you the most diligent of his listeners.

Your internal *sufferings* <note>original: "pâtimens". An archaic term derived from "pâtir" (to suffer), referring here to a spiritualized or passive endurance of the soul's trials.</note> caused by charity—can you believe them to be of no use to your friend? <note>In this mystical context, the "friend" refers to the Divine Presence or God, who is portrayed as a close companion to the soul.</note>

It is not too much to say that they bring you closer to God, that they please God, in that they associate you with Him, and that they make you like His love.

This is the work; this is the first degree of the work. Let all nations hear me!

May they become pure enough to feel the internal *sufferings* of charity.

I see two words written on this tree of life: Sword and love.

By the sword of the word I will subdue all the enemies of my God, I will bind them, and I will prevent them from causing pain to my God.

Through love, I will zealously beseech Him to pour into me a ray of His charity;

And to grant that I might relieve Him by taking upon myself some of the *sufferings* of His love.

Be not offended, O my God, by the loftiness of this idea; it is You who brought it to life in my heart;

### 7.

<term>Interpreters</term> of mythology <note>likely referring to "mythographers" or scholars who sought to explain ancient myths through science or history</note>, why do you say that it only veiled the course of the stars, and the laws of material and corruptible nature?

What proportion would there be, in that case, between the figure and the thing represented? Is allegory not useless when it is superior to its object?

Does it not cease to be allegory? Yes, then it is a power, and it acts by open force.

But a new obstacle arises: mythology and physics would be in dispute.

Mythology, to be admissible, should at least rest upon the active principles of nature;

This refers to the "Prime Mover" (Primum Mobile), an Aristotelian and scholastic concept of God as the primary cause of all motion in the universe.</note> of all that is.

Thus everything is individual, and yet everything is but one. Who then is this **Immense Being** who, from his impenetrable center, sees all beings, the stars, the entire universe form but a single point of his incommensurable sphere?

However, I saw there only the order and the arrangement of beings. But hardly had I fixed my sight upon their *action*, than the picture grew larger.

<term>Universal source</term> — the divine origin from which all life flows.
<term>Inexhaustible fire</term> — a common mystical metaphor for the soul or the divine energy that drives creation.
<term>Kingdoms of nature</term> — the hierarchical levels of the physical world (mineral, plant, animal).
<term>Prime Mover</term> — God as the ultimate source of all movement and change.

### 47.

**When** will you cease to believe that you have no indication of the things that preceded you, and that it is impossible for you to ever have the slightest trace of them?

Listen: without taking refuge in conventional and arbitrary things, even if you were not just yourself, you are not at all devoid of ideas of distributive justice <term>justice distributive: the principle of giving to each what is due to them, which Saint-Martin views as an innate moral compass</term>.

When you harm your fellow man, there are indeed some moments when you feel that you would suffer if he treated you the same way; and if your prejudice and your passion rest for a moment, they allow you to see that you have gone astray.

Where does this sense of the balance come from, to which you yield in your inner conscience <term>for-intérieur: literally "inner forum"; the private, internal court of one’s own conscience and soul</term>, even if you do not always have the strength to be faithful to it in your conduct?

This is a spark of the fire that shone in a time of which you have no memory. It is a monument, an antiquity <note>original: "une antique." Here used as a noun meaning a relic or artifact from an ancient era.</note>, which sets you on the path of the sciences of its time. It is a germ <note>original: "germe." A seed or life-spark containing the potential for future growth.</note> of the plants...

### 48.

To what harsh struggles do the obstacles we bring with us at birth expose us! It is not by avoiding them that we will gain the victory. They are sent to us so that our constancy and our bravery may make us recover what is being withheld from our inheritance. <note>In the author's philosophy, the "inheritance" refers to the original divine powers and status humanity held before the "Fall" or its descent into the material world.</note>

What are our temporal wars, <note>original: "guerres temporelles." These are worldly conflicts limited by time, as opposed to the eternal spiritual struggle of the soul.</note> where it is only a matter of pursuing the conquest of a country and a citadel that are before our eyes? Here, our soul must, through its efforts, produce and create, in a sense, what has been stolen from us.

The universal inheritance had been distributed to the entire human family; each individual family was to receive its portion. Each individual was to receive, along with life, all the aid, all the weapons we need to fulfill our task. <term>emploi: this refers to the "ministry" or spiritual duty that every human being is meant to perform in the restoration of the universe.</term>

If this inheritance was not guarded for us, if part of it was allowed to be stolen, we are nonetheless obliged to perform our work, as if we had received everything.

This is the secret misfortune of so many mortals; this is the state of violence. <note>original: "état de violence." For Saint-Martin, the "state of violence" is the unnatural condition of the soul being imprisoned in a material body, where it is constantly buffeted by forces that do not belong to its true home.</note> Inheritances are confounded; they pass into foreign and illegitimate hands.

### 49.

Let man separate his soul from all the objects that surround him, and they will no longer be anything to him; he only experiences them through his *life*, which alone creates all the value of things for him.

Who other than himself would be the true author of his wanderings and his illusions, since he has within him a principle of truth and *life*, and since he can only find in dead beings <note>The author refers to the physical, material world as "dead beings" or "dead matter," which only appears "alive" or meaningful because the human soul projects its own vitality onto it.</note> the *life* that he himself brings to them?

Wretched man, you can, by turning your soul away, prevent divine life itself from penetrating you; you are not the creator of *life*, but you are its arbiter and its minister in your domain. <note>In the author's mystical system, man acts as a "minister" or steward—a middle-manager of sorts between the Divine and the physical world—with the free will to either block or transmit spiritual light.</note>

What a difference in sensation when he places himself under the <term>supreme action: a state of being in direct alignment with divine will or spiritual influence</term>, or when he descends to inferior objects! They often cause him joy, it is true, because he brings his *life* to them, and because the feeling of *life* is always a sweet affection for all beings.

But probe this joy: you will find it convulsive, and resting upon relations; it will secretly shudder to encounter objects of comparison, which constrain it, condemn it, and destroy it. <note>The author suggests that earthly joy is "convulsive" (unstable and fleeting) because it depends on comparing ourselves to others or temporary circumstances, whereas spiritual joy is self-sustaining.</note>

### 53.

Even assuming that the most skillful physician cannot foresee the shifts in health of a healthy man, he can foresee the entire course of a disease once it has been determined <note>The author uses a medical analogy: just as a doctor understands how a specific disease will progress once it starts, God understands the trajectory of human history once a moral "principle" or choice has been set in motion.</note>.

### 58.

Yes, Lord, it is possible for us to still sing the song of Moses and that of the lamb; <note>An allusion to Revelation 15:3: "And they sing the song of Moses... and the song of the Lamb," symbolizing the harmony between the Old and New Covenants and the soul's victory over the material world.</note> let us always give one more impulse to our soul, and it will produce for us all that we lack.

Cowardice is a lack of faith in the one who formed us. It is through cowardice, and never through powerlessness, that we are defeated. I shall say henceforth to the human soul:

> *Let us no longer count the delays of time.*

### 60.

I was praying, and I felt the **chaos** <term>chaos: here referring to the disordered, noisy state of the human mind before it achieves spiritual stillness</term> of human thoughts abandon me and descend below me. A pure light rose gently from the heart of my soul and spread throughout my whole being.

*Let there be light, and there was light.* <note>original: "Que la lumière paroisse, et la lumière parut." This is a translation of the Latin biblical command "Fiat lux, et lux facta est" from Genesis 1:3.</note>

What happened, mighty God, when you commanded the universe to be born, and the light to spread over all your works? Their principle of life was in **inertia**; light struck upon them, but they could have no feeling of it; they were like a child asleep in the middle of the day.

Your **word** penetrated them; they emerged from their sleep, and each went to take the post you had assigned to them in the universe.

By rising to this degree of activity, they let those who were refractory to your word, and who did not open their organs <note>In the mystical tradition of the author, "organs" often refers to internal spiritual senses rather than just physical body parts.</note> to your light, fall below them.

The **stars** are like so many diamonds that you detached from your crown, and that you let fall from your throne into the enclosure of the universe, so that it might gain an idea of your wealth and your majesty.

### 64.

Is the spirit of man weakened, is it more contained, or does it operate in regions more invisible than in the past? It seems no longer to have even the strength to commit significant crimes.

The <term>ancient peoples</term> <note>original: "anciens peuples"; Saint-Martin refers to the civilizations of antiquity, often seen in his philosophy as possessing more direct—if often misused—spiritual power than modern man.</note> were horribly corrupt; their strength extended from the underworld even to the heavens.

Thus the <term>celestial powers</term> <note>original: "puissances célestes"; the angelic or divine forces that govern the order of the universe.</note> set themselves in motion. God shook the roots and the pillars of nature. He commanded the waters to cover the face of the earth. He laid bare the foundations of the world.

When the criminal powers of peoples began to weaken, celestial vengeances likewise subsided. Threats took the place of these vengeances, and the <term>prophets</term> <note>original: "prophètes"; the messengers of the Old Testament who transitioned the divine interaction from physical cataclysms to moral and spiritual warnings.</note> were charged with frightening the nations.

->77.<-

To what ideas have they reduced themselves with their systems! They have said that there was no evil on earth, and that what appeared to be a disorder in particular produced universal order.

### 81.

My songs, why are you not like torrents of the fire of the spirit! You are yet only the fruit of my desires, so that this spirit may not be separated from man.

They are not the sharp sword that might put the enemy of the Lord to flight. They are not the light and sharp arrow that flies afar to strike the destructive lion or the bird of prey.

### 85.

**All** religions have a cult and ceremonies; all religious doctrines have tangible practices <note>original: "pratiques sensibles"; rituals that are perceptible to the senses, which Saint-Martin views as necessary supports for spiritual ideas.</note>.

### 94.

How could I doubt that man is tasked with performing his own work <term>œuvre: This refers to the Great Work (Magnum Opus) of spiritual reintegration, a central concept in Martinist philosophy where man must actively labor to restore his original divine state.</term> and creating his own pleasures? Why must God, necessarily and eternally, confine Himself to the contemplation of Himself? It is because there is no other being who is worthy of His gaze.

### 122.

Let us no longer ask what the object of science <note>In this context, "science" does not refer to modern empirical study, but to *sacred science*—the systematic knowledge of spiritual truths and the divine order.</note> is; it is nothing other than to untangle the pure from the impure, so as to lead us to the unmixed region.

->131.<-

Followers of poetry, if you were to read the Holy Scriptures, what wonders would they not offer you! There you would see stones that speak in temples built with blood. You would see the warriors of iniquity descending to the depths of the abyss, resting there with their heads leaning upon their swords. <note>Saint-Martin often draws on the vivid, sometimes terrifying imagery of the Old Testament prophets (like Ezekiel) to illustrate spiritual truths.</note>

There you would see the Divinity fleeing from his temples, no longer finding any room there because of the multitude of idols.

There you would see divine charity itself unloosing the bits <note>Original: "le mors." This refers to the bit of a horse's bridle, symbolizing the harsh restraint or control over a person.</note> of the transgressors and the slaves, and presenting them with nourishment with her own hand.

There you would see sublimity, strength, and variety; you would have only the embarrassment of riches in your choices, and never the fear of scarcity. But the hand of wisdom blinds your profane <note>Profane: in this context, meaning "secular" or "uninitiated," rather than "disrespectful."</note> eyes when you traverse this rich and vast meadow.

<vocab>poetry, Holy Scriptures, Divinity, divine charity, wisdom</vocab>

Without this, the flowers you would gather would serve only as food for your pride and as victims to the prostitution of human opinions. Holy Scripture was given to enrich the heart and the intelligence of man. ### 132.

You believe Him <note>Referring to God, the "Eternal" mentioned later in the text.</note> alone and isolated, because there is no other God but Him. How could He be alone! His thought knows no interval, and all His thoughts are creations.

Is He, like man, infirm and limited? Does He agitate Himself, as man does, within the narrow circle of His own thoughts? And does He see them, like man, continually flowing back upon themselves and becoming entangled in their own confusion and impotence?

He thinks; and at every thought, beings emerge in crowds from His bosom, just as the innumerable rays of light continually emerge from that brilliant star <note>Saint-Martin likely refers to the Sun here, used as a traditional mystical symbol for the visible sanctuary of Divine light.</note> which was given to Him as a sanctuary.

These legions of beings follow one another like the waves of the sea, or like the numerous clouds driven through the air by the impetuosity of the winds. They all have diverse functions; and they hasten with ardor to fulfill them.

They reflect the dazzling brightness of their eternal source, and form, like temples placed from space to space throughout immensity, so that immensity may be filled with the praises and the glory of the Eternal.

They temper this brightness for the eyes <note>The text breaks off here; Saint-Martin is likely describing how these created beings act as intermediaries, softening the overwhelming light of God so it can be perceived by lesser creatures.</note>

# MAN

have interaction <note>original: "commerce." In this context, it refers to social, intellectual, or spiritual exchange between individuals.</note> with one another? Writing, when they are separated; speech, when they can hear each other; action, when they see one another.

The friend who gives it to us, thinks it; why would he not follow all these progressions? Why would he not contain **substances in seed**, **substances in growth**, **substances in fruition**? <note>original: "substances en germe, en végétation, en production." The author uses botanical metaphors to describe the unfolding of thought from a hidden potential to a visible result.</note>

Everything is a picture in the works of thought. It never presents itself to us except under a sensory form, because everything is complete in the source that produces it.

This sensory form is its writing. But we only write to one another when we are separated. These are the **substances in seed**. . . Can we not hear the voices of men in the midst of darkness, and without seeing them! These are the **substances in growth**. . . . .

But there is a third degree! We see men act when they are near us and when the light shines upon them! These are the **substances in fruition**. . . . .

It is therefore true that we write to men, that we speak to them, and that we act before them, though they perceive it so little; just as it is true that all these things occur materially before children. <note>The author suggests that just as children witness adult activities without understanding their depth, humanity witnesses divine or spiritual "actions" through nature without fully grasping their significance.</note>

It seems that in sacred dwellings <note>original: "demeures sacrées." # MAN

However distinguished a genius may be, even in matters of the spirit, he will only be able to sustain himself as long as he dwells with piety.

Is it not then sublime enough for him, this idea of being able to feel and utter that we have God for our father; and that, by this word alone, we ennoble the entire human family, while simultaneously reuniting all its members through the bonds of love and brotherhood?

Is it not sublime enough for him, this idea of feeling that he must not pronounce this word "father" before his God, if there is a man of whom he is not the brother and the friend?

Pray, pray, until you feel yourself pursued by the intense longing for this delight <note>original: "concupiscence de cette jouissance." In this mystical context, the author uses "concupiscence" to describe a driving spiritual appetite or a deep, holy craving for divine communion, rather than its more common association with carnal desire.</note>. That is the life of your being.

Come forth, divine branches, you who are as if begotten by prayer. Cover with your shade the paths that lead to the temple of the Lord; so that the nations may know that the ways leading to the Lord are sweet beyond all our thoughts.

### 165.

The middle of the times was the interval between justice and mercy: thus Paul, following Habakkuk, announces to us that the middle of the times was the chosen time <note>A reference to Habakkuk 3:2, "in the midst of the years," often interpreted by mystics as the era of Christ or the moment of spiritual awakening.</note>.

### 166.

You agree then, learned men of letters, that the <term>sublime</term> <note>The "Sublime" was a major topic in 18th-century aesthetics, referring to an artistic or natural quality that produces an overwhelming sense of awe or greatness beyond measurement.</note> is undefinable? You depict for us different genres of the sublime; you cite for us the sublime passages of our poets.

You cite for us the response of that mother, to whom one spoke of the sacrifice of Isaac: *God would not have asked for that sacrifice from a mother* <note>original: "Dieu n’auroit pas demandé ce sacrifice-là à une mère"</note>; without paying attention to the fact that Isaac, being the son of faith, could not be compared to a son of the senses and of matter.

You cite for us the loftiness of those warriors who, at the sight of the mausoleum of a great general, draw their sabers and sharpen them on the marble of his tomb.

All these pictures animate us, warm us, and do not instruct us. We feel it, the sublime; we feel how little it is within our dependence. Why then is it impossible to define? Here is the reason:

### 168.

### 171.

I will spend my nights in sleeplessness. The great wound <note>The "great wound" refers to the spiritual Fall of humanity and its separation from the Divine, a central theme in Saint-Martin's thought.</note> will keep me awake, and will prevent my eyelids from knowing a moment of rest.

### 210.

The SPIRIT of man often asks himself what purpose animals could serve in the plan of creation?

Do we not see in them some scattered signs of the virtues that are recommended to us? Of prudence, courage, fidelity, attachment, skill, and <term>resourcefulness</term><note>original: "industrie" — In this 18th-century context, this refers to the natural cleverness or diligent effort animals use to survive and provide for themselves, rather than modern manufacturing.</note>, to combat the evils that afflict them?

Do you not know that, since the <term>disorder</term><note>original: "le désordre" — A term frequently used in mystical philosophy to describe the Fall of Man and the resulting chaotic state of the material world.</note>, Wisdom has presented to man models more useful and more powerful than animals could ever be?

Fix your gaze upon these divine and living models; instruct yourselves by their example; nourish yourselves with their strength: and you will have nothing to regret in the plans that are half-erased.

->217.<-

How long will you be at odds with yourself? Your heart would like to find joy; it would like to surrender to the sweet impressions that the very feeling of its existence suggests to it.

### 218.

Do I not see three degrees for man? He is either above his measure, at its level, or below it.

Is he at the level, and does he obtain in proportion? He will pass peaceful days. Is he above? There is only triumph and enjoyment for him. But this degree is not to be sought on earth.

Who are those who suffer the most? Those who have received a great measure from above, and who are forced to wait elsewhere to fill it. These are the ones who will be comforted: for they cannot fail to weep abundantly.

Lord, are not those whom you choose for your work usually victims of the **profound idea**<note>original: "idée profonde" — In Saint-Martin's thought, this refers to an innate, deep-seated spiritual intuition or realization of God that transcends mere intellectual belief.</note> that you give them of yourself?

They encounter nothing on earth but opposition to this profound idea; every day they see the **living thing**<note>original: "la chose vive" — Likely referring to the spirit or the true life of the soul.</note> sacrificed to that which languishes and decomposes of its own accord.

### 226.

JEREMIAH <note>A reference to the biblical book of Jeremiah 10:24: "O Lord, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing."</note> thus asked you, Lord, *to punish him in your justice, and not in your fury, for fear of reducing him to nothing!* These then are the two ways that you use to punish man! You are forced to be severe with him when it is not enough for him that you be just.

But you also have two ways to communicate your favors to him. One is your mercy and the other is your love. If God is so terrible in his justice, what must he not be in his severity or in his fury!

His fury is for the impious; his justice is for the disobedient; his mercy is for the weak, whose faults he is willing to forget. His love is for those in whom he even stops and prevents them <note>The word "prevents" here is used in the older sense of "prevenient grace"—divine grace that precedes human decision and acts upon the soul to steer it away from sin before it occurs.</note>.

If God is so gentle in his mercy, what must he then be in his love! Men, you always demand more than the measure. God always demands less, if he sees that he is sought and loved. But it is only for the small and the simple to hear these truths.

Is belief not our natural state? Who is more disposed to faith than the child? This is also because he is closest to the state of nature. <note>For Saint-Martin, the "state of nature" is not a primitive or animalistic condition, but rather the original, uncorrupted spiritual state of man before the Fall, characterized by a natural, intuitive connection to the Divine.</note>

### 247.

What is the place, what is the object from which man will draw satisfaction, if he does not bring the seed and the principle of it himself? <note>original: "germe et le principe" — Saint-Martin emphasizes that spiritual fulfillment is an internal quality that a person must project onto the world, rather than something extracted from external things.</note>

And if he brings the seed and the principle with him, what is the place, what is the object, from which he will not draw satisfaction?

How shall the priest live by the altar of life, if he does not bring there a ray that attracts the spirit of life? And if he carries within himself that which attracts the spirit of life, can he not revivify even the altar of death? <note>The "altar of death" refers to the material world, which is spiritually "dead" unless animated by the human soul.</note>

Know then, deceived man, what character you were meant to carry in the universe. It is you who, as the depository of life, transmitted the sanction <note>original: "sanction" — here meaning the divine authority or seal of approval that gives beings their true meaning and order.</note> to all beings.

They were nothing to you, if you did not begin by animating them with the sacred fire, which you had the right to go and take from the altar of life.

Today, do you spread life around you? Do you carry it into the objects that approach you? Do you not seem to wait from them for the satisfactions and the life that you ought to give to them?

And yet you seek to extinguish in them the ray of fire, which is granted to them by your nature. You transpose all substances; you find that nothing is in its place. <note>By seeking fulfillment in material objects rather than spiritual ones, Man disrupts the natural order of the universe, treating "substances" as ends in themselves rather than reflections of the Divine.</note>

### 252.

**When** will action be at its full? When will the rocky masses be reduced to powder? Is it not the cessation of action that has petrified everything? Is it not the rebirth of action that must restore life and mobility?

The stillness of action brings the color of darkness; the rebirth of action brings back the color of light.

How vivid it is, this color of light! You are nothing beside it, whiteness of lilies! You are even lesser still, O you, whiteness of the snow, for you possess nothing bright enough to reflect the true color of light.

Thus, you reflect only its image. You are the color of man washed of his sins. But you do not represent man regenerated in the activity of life.

It is boiling bronze <note>original: "airain" — a term often used in mystical literature to signify a strength that has been purified and tempered by extreme heat</note> in the furnace that represents man regenerated in the activity of life. This man is swept away by the torrent of life. He is stirred by it, he is filled by it; the divine fire becomes one with him.

Go wash yourselves in the pool; <note>original: "la piscine" — an allusion to the biblical Pool of Bethesda (John 5:2-4), where the sick sought healing when the waters were stirred by an angel.</note> go renew yourselves in the spirit. Can your body itself not be healed of some wound to the point of no longer feeling the slightest sensation of its pain?

There was a time when only one man at a time could enter this pool; today, all can throw themselves into it together: and the Angel has been ordered to stir its water continually for all those of the human family who wish to present themselves there.

Man was sent under a second law. He departed from unity to halt the binary law.

He existed in a second law, in relation to his emanation;

### 259.

It is not enough for me to open my eyes; its light <note>Likely referring to the "living wisdom" or "Principle" mentioned on the previous page.</note> must help me to unravel what I encounter.

His tongue has sharpened; it has become keen, like the sword of the Lord; it has encircled all the globes, it has revealed the fruits, and all the substances that compose them.

It has cast down those flaming and smoke-filled clouds that emerge from these inner retreats. It has reduced everything to orderly designs; and vagueness and uncertainty have vanished.

Who is the man who has not allowed a mold to form within himself, where everything comes to take the same impression? Anything that has not taken the shape of this mold is beyond his reach; he can do nothing but condemn it.

Respect the leaders. If God sends them and they are ignorant, it is a trial for the Church. If they come of their own accord, one must pray for them, so that the <term>supreme hand</term> <note>A reference to God's direct intervention or Providence.</note> may heal them of their folly.

But as for us, let us strip ourselves bare, if we wish to be superbly clothed, and if we wish to be without anxiety regarding the fruits of our thoughts.

# OF DESIRE

It is not to know God to believe that the reach of His arm is shortened <note>original: "la mesure de son bras se raccourcisse." This is a biblical allusion to Isaiah 59:1: "Surely the arm of the Lord is not too short to save." We ought to lighten and strip ourselves down here below, yet we do nothing but encumber ourselves under the accumulated wrappings of impurity and illusion.

We ought to undergo a salutary trial here below, yet we postpone it to another region. Then we shall have two to undergo at once, without knowing if we shall be in a state to bear them.

How are we born? Stripped of everything! The goods and the pleasures that come to us are a free gift granted to us, and which [the Divine] is then willing to receive back from us as an offering.

Our very children—why not look upon them in some way as a kind of boarder <note>original: "pensionnaires." In this context, it suggests that children are temporary residents or guests entrusted to parents by God, rather than being the parents' "property."</note> whom God gives us to raise for Him?

Children of Israel <note>In Saint-Martin’s "Martinist" philosophy, "Children of Israel" often refers metaphorically to all spiritual seekers or "men of desire" who are striving to return to their divine origin, rather than strictly the ethnic or national group.</note>, let us no longer complain of adversities, let us no longer complain even of injustices; they are so many rungs offered to us, to help us climb upon the pyre and upon the altar of sacrifice.

->283.<-

**HOW** many times have writers repeated the primitive prevarications <note>original: "prévarications primitives." This term refers to the "Fall" or the original deviation of humanity from the divine path. Turn your thoughts toward the great jubilee <note>The biblical Jubilee refers to a year of total liberation and the return of property; here, it signifies the soul's restoration to its original divine state.</note>, and see how brief and rapid is the interval found between the completion of the seven powers of the spirit and the destruction of the number of iniquity.

The fire of hope has issued from the heart of this marvelous work: it has set the man of courage ablaze; it has come to set the soul on fire in the midst of its chains.

The prison where it <note>The soul (l'âme), which is feminine in French.</note> was held has been shaken by a violent tremor; its guards were terrified by it.

Its chains fell away of their own accord, the doors of its prison opened; it walked in freedom and went to rejoin its brothers.

This is the fate that awaits the Word <note>Refers to *la Parole*, the divine creative faculty inherent in man that Saint-Martin believes must be "re-integrated" or freed from the depths of the Fall.</note> when it has made every effort to emerge from the abyss; and those who had cast it there, and who wished to keep it there, will be sent to their punishment.

<summary>This page describes the spiritual liberation of the soul and the divine "Word" from the bondage of sin and material existence, likening the process to an escape from a guarded prison. It emphasizes that the internal "fire of hope" and the pursuit of divine "true numbers" are the catalysts for this restoration to freedom.</summary>

### 299.

Where is the principle of the science of man? <note>Saint-Martin refers here to *la science de l’homme*, a mystical study of humanity’s divine origin and spiritual nature, rather than physical biology.</note> Is it not found within himself and very close to him? His misfortune is to go looking for it outside of himself, and in objects that cannot reactivate his true germ <term>germ: the "divine spark" or innate spiritual potential that Saint-Martin believes is buried within human nature since the Fall</term>.

And then, what mistakes does he not make regarding the classes <note>Likely referring to the "classes" of spiritual beings or the hierarchical levels of the created universe.</note>? Instead of working assiduously to know them, he does nothing but transpose their gradations.

<margin>X</margin>
He could devote his first steps to employing natural things with precision, with the eye of the spirit, and with continual attention to the place, the time, and the quality of beings.

But what are you, marvelous effects of nature? You are but the consequence of the laws established in the beginning. You should only reveal yourselves to man in order to raise him to a superior order, of which you are the image.

Thus, your strength and your invariable laws have an admirable power to lead us to this high goal.

For if monsters <note>In the 18th century, "monsters" referred to biological anomalies. Saint-Martin argues that because these deviations cannot usually reproduce their own kind ("engender"), it proves that the laws of nature are fixed and governed by a higher divine "convention."</note> were to engender, would the eternal convention not be overturned?

Holy convention, happy is he who approaches you with a pure intention,

<summary>Saint-Martin argues that the path to true wisdom lies within the human spirit rather than the external material world, which only serves as a reflection of a higher divine order. He suggests that the stability of natural laws—even the inability of "monsters" to disrupt the biological order—points toward a holy, eternal "convention."</summary>

<margin>X</margin>
At the moment of the crime <note>original: *le crime*; Saint-Martin uses this term to describe the "Fall" or the original spiritual rebellion that led to the creation of the material world.</note>, all the universes became opaque and subject to gravity <term>gravity: *pesanteur*; in Martinist philosophy, this refers to the denseness of matter that traps the spirit, as opposed to the "lightness" of the divine realm</term>: the crime has, as it were, coagulated the words of life; it has rendered all of nature mute.

Human posterity, you have abused the silence of the Word <note>original: *la parole*; here referring to the divine Logos or the creative power of God.</note> to deprave yourself even further, believing that there was no longer any Word near you, nor above you!

But is the Word of the Lord not a double-edged sword? Is it not a living sword? Silence and a mute being, such as nature, are to it acts of violence and a temporary state.

The Lord has spoken, his voice triumphs...

<note>This section emphasizes that the "silence" of God in the material world is not an absence, but a temporary condition caused by humanity's spiritual descent. The "Word" remains active and will eventually restore the original order.</note>

<summary>Saint-Martin explains that the material world and the laws of gravity are "coagulated" results of the Fall, rendering nature mute. He warns humanity not to mistake this silence for the absence of the Divine Word, which remains a living force ready to restore the supreme glory.</summary>

...and triumphs over the powers of crime <note>original: *le crime*; Saint-Martin uses this term to refer to the original spiritual rebellion or the "Fall" that separated humanity from the divine.</note>. Silence is abolished. All points of the universe are transformed into living tongues.

Oh night, you rush away with the silence; can darkness exist beside the word of the Eternal? Nature has become as brilliant as the sun, because she has become, like it, the tabernacle <note>A "tabernacle" is a dwelling place or a sanctuary; here, nature is restored to its role as a container for divine presence.</note> of the word.

But the word, upon awakening, will divide all worlds into two classes, just as of old the Hebrews were divided on Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 27-28, where the Israelites stood on two mountains: Gerizim to pronounce blessings and Ebal to pronounce curses for those who broke the Law.</note>; and the voices of Ebal will ceaselessly pronounce the curse against the enemies of the law of the Lord.

Impious man, careless man, place yourself in this terrible moment; there is no longer space nor time for you.

You no longer have, as you do here below, the resource of darkness and silence to preserve you from the dread that the light and the word of the Lord would cause you. You are going to be pursued by the light and by the word.

Like the guilty man here below, abandoned to fatal evils or the sword of justice; you will hear your blood and all your substances take up speech to curse you, and to curse all your acts of iniquity.

Man of desire <note>original: *Homme de desir*; Saint-Martin’s signature term for the spiritual seeker who yearns to restore their original divine nature.</note>, strive to reach the mountain of blessing, give rebirth within yourself to the true word.

### 301.

Superficial observers <note>Original: *légers observateurs*; those who study the physical world without considering its spiritual foundations.</note>, my pictures will not appear worthy of your gaze. I have not separated from my meditations, as you have, the powerful Being by whom everything exists.

It is by excluding Him that you have claimed to make us know the truth. He is truth itself. What am I saying—He alone is truth. What could you have found without Him?

Let the souls to whom you strive to teach a foreign language <note>Saint-Martin views materialist or purely rationalist philosophy as a "foreign language" that is alien to the soul's true nature.</note> come here to relearn their own without fatigue, and let them forget yours forever!

You provide some pleasures to their minds by offering them those glimmers that the benevolent and fruitful wisdom allows to shine even into the furthest branches of nature.

But these are like the pale glimmers of a dying lamp, like those flames li-

<meta>This page concludes the final chapter of "The Man of Desire." It picks up mid-sentence from the previous page’s metaphor, contrasting the fleeting, dying "flames" of materialist philosophy with the eternal "source" of divine light.</meta>

<page-num>256</page-num>
<header>MAN</header>

...flames that one sees detaching at intervals, and vanishing into the air, because they are separated from their source <note>Original: *foyer*; meaning a hearth, center, or focal point of light and heat.</note>.

I have preferred to fix the eyes of my brothers upon the source itself, and upon the oil of joy <note>A biblical reference (Isaiah 61:3) to the spiritual comfort and anointing given to the faithful.</note> which has served as an anointing for the chosen of my God.

This is the only means within my power to bring them profitable help; others will advance the reign of my God further than I, through their works and through their power.

I have received as my portion only the desire to sing His glory, to unveil the iniquitous lies of His adversaries, and to encourage my fellow men to direct their steps toward this sanctuary <note>Original: *asyle*; a place of refuge or a sacred retreat.</note> of true and ineffable delights.

If I have only the widow's mite <note>Original: *le denier de la veuve*; referring to the story in Mark 12:42 where a poor widow gives all she has, which is worth more in spirit than the large sums given by the wealthy.</note> to offer them to help them make the journey of life, I implore them not to reject it without having tested its value.

It is with sweet consolation that I shall see them gather these feeble fruits of the desires of a simple man who loved them.

May the virtue of their hearts, may the piety of the ages, be the funeral hymn that shall be sung forever over my grave!

I shall hear it in the sleep of peace, and I shall return all homage for it to my God.

->T H E   E N D.<-

<summary>In this concluding passage, Saint-Martin humbles himself, offering his writings as a modest "widow's mite" intended to guide readers toward divine truth. He ends with a prayer that the virtue of future generations might serve as his ultimate funeral hymn.</summary>
<keywords>Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin, mysticism, oil of joy, widow's mite, spiritual desire, humility, divine source, funeral hymn</keywords>
